pronunciation.note: Kotoshironushi is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. He is a son of Ōkuninushi and a key figure in the transfer of the land to Amaterasu's descendants.

domains.title: Lord Who Substitutes
domains.subtitle: Oracle, Fishing, and the Transfer of the Land
domains.lead: Kotoshironushi is the son of Ōkuninushi who, according to the Kojiki, surrendered the central land of reed plains to the heavenly descendants of Amaterasu. A god of oracles and fishing, he withdrew to the sea and became identified in later tradition with the fortune god Ebisu.

cards.name: Land Transfer

cards.name: Oracle God

cards.name: Fishing Deity
cards.desc: Like Ebisu, he withdrew to the sea and governed its bounty.

cards.name: Ebisu Link

mythology.lead: Kotoshironushi's mythology centers on the peaceful transfer of sovereignty from the earthly kami to the heavenly line.

myths.title: The Cession of the Land
myths.text: When Amaterasu sent her grandson Ninigi to rule the earth, the earthly kami Ōkuninushi resisted. After negotiations and divine pressure, Ōkuninushi asked his son Kotoshironushi for advice. Kotoshironushi declared that the land should be surrendered to the heavenly descendants, and he withdrew to the sea. His voluntary submission made the peaceful transfer possible.

myths.title: Oracle at Miwa
myths.text: The Nihon Shoki associates Kotoshironushi with the Miwa area and with oracular divination. His withdrawal to the sea and identification with marine fortune reflect his role as a mediator between land and water, old order and new.

myths.title: Kotoshironushi and Ebisu
myths.text: In popular devotion, Kotoshironushi merged with Hiruko and other sea figures to become Ebisu, the smiling god of fishermen and merchants. This synthesis shows how minor mythological figures could be gathered into a single, beloved deity.

lore.syncretism: Kotoshironushi is a nodal figure connecting the land-transfer myth, oracle cults, and the later Ebisu tradition. He represents the old order's willing surrender and the sea's continuing bounty. His absorption into Ebisu is one of the clearest cases of mythological condensation in Japanese folk religion.
lore.culturalLegacy: Kotoshironushi is rarely worshipped independently today, but his legacy lives in Ebisu and in the story of how the imperial line gained the land without total war. He is remembered as the son who advised surrender for the greater good.
lore.extendedMeditation: Kotoshironushi teaches that sovereignty can pass peacefully. His withdrawal is not defeat but wisdom: sometimes the greater power yields to the new order so that life — fishing, trade, worship — can continue.
lore.archaeology: Kotoshironushi is associated with the Miwa area and with shrines honoring Ōkuninushi's lineage. His identification with Ebisu means his material traces are embedded in the broader cult of the Seven Gods of Fortune.
